messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Mehta was 32 when she came for treatment, a single South Asian American woman serving on the city council in a large urban district. She described the beginning of her problems as the afternoon a man-made disaster struck during a public community event she was attending in her official role. The gathering had been routine at first: folding chairs set out in rows, staff moving between tables, residents waiting to speak with local officials. Then there was a sudden human-caused blast that shattered the ordinary feel of the room in an instant. People screamed and surged toward the exits. Chairs scraped and overturned. Priya remembered the terror of not knowing whether there would be another explosion, whether the person responsible was still nearby, and whether the crowd itself would become as dangerous as the blast. In those moments, what fixed itself most strongly in her mind was the necessity of finding a way out immediately and of reading people around her for signs of danger.

In the weeks that followed, she did not talk about the event as something over. She had come to believe that it had shown her the truth about the world: that danger could appear without warning in places that were supposed to be safe, and that anyone who let down their guard was being naive. She was certain she had to stay alert all the time, because “you never know what can happen next.” This was not an abstract belief for her. It shaped the way she entered every room. At council meetings, before she could focus on the agenda, she found herself locating side doors, hallways, stairwells, and any space behind the dais that might offer a quick exit. If she was invited to speak at a neighborhood center she had never visited, she often delayed giving an answer or declined outright, telling herself that in an unfamiliar place she could not properly assess the danger.

Her work made these habits especially visible. As a city council member, much of her day involved public buildings, evening forums, and meetings with people she did not know. She no longer walked into these settings with the easy confidence colleagues remembered. She scanned constantly: who was standing near the door, whose expression looked off, who seemed agitated, who was watching her too closely. During constituent events she kept track of where security staff were positioned and whether there was enough open space to move if she needed to. She described not feeling settled anywhere until she had identified an escape route. Even then, her attention remained divided, one part of her listening to residents and another sweeping the room for threat.

Night was markedly worse. She said she could not feel safe after dark in the way she once had. Evening meetings, which were unavoidable in local politics, became ordeals. The darkened parking garages, street corners outside municipal buildings, and the sense of reduced visibility all left her more tense and watchful. If an event ran late, she noticed herself becoming increasingly keyed up, checking who was entering and leaving, gauging distances to exits, and mentally rehearsing how she would get out if something happened. What frightened her most was the feeling that nighttime concealed intentions and limited her options.

Over months, her life narrowed around these calculations. She began avoiding unfamiliar venues whenever she could, steering staff toward city hall or other buildings she knew well. She also started avoiding situations that put her body under stress. She worried that if her heart was pounding or her breathing became labored, she would be less able to detect danger or act quickly. As a result, she cut back on physical activity and passed on events that required rushing between locations or standing for long periods in dense crowds. The consequence at work was subtle but real: colleagues noticed she was less willing to appear in new parts of the district, and some outreach opportunities were lost because she would not agree to attend unless she could first understand the layout and exits.

By the time she sought help, Priya was exhausted by the constant effort of being on guard. She still believed the world was dangerous and that vigilance was necessary, but she was beginning to see how fully that belief had taken over her days and nights. She came in after declining yet another evening event in an unfamiliar community space and feeling a surge of shame afterward, aware that her job required presence in exactly the settings she now found hardest to tolerate. She said she wanted help because she was tired of living as if every room needed an escape plan before she could breathe normally. At the same time, she was deeply afraid that if she stopped scanning, stopped watching people, or let herself feel physically off-balance, she would miss the next sign of catastrophe and be caught unprepared.
